{{Short description|Topological continuum undefinable as the union of any two proper subcontinua}}
{{For|the indecomposability attributed to the real line by constructive mathematics|Indecomposability (constructive mathematics)}}
[[Image:ContinuBJK.svg|thumb|upright=0.8|The first four stages of the construction of the bucket handle as the limit of a series of nested intersections]]

In [[point-set topology]], an '''indecomposable continuum''' is a [[continuum (topology)|continuum]] that is indecomposable, i.e. that cannot be expressed as the union of any two of its [[Subset#Definitions|proper]] subcontinua. In 1910, [[L. E. J. Brouwer]] was the first to describe an indecomposable continuum. 

Indecomposable continua have been used by topologists as a source of [[counterexample]]s. They also occur in [[dynamical systems]].

==Definitions==

A ''continuum'' <math>C</math> is a nonempty [[Compact space|compact]] [[Connected space|connected]] [[metric space]]. The [[Arc (topology)|arc]], the [[n-sphere|''n''-sphere]], and the [[Hilbert cube]] are examples of [[Connected_space#Path_connectedness|path-connected]] continua; the [[topologist's sine curve]] is an example of a continuum that is not path-connected.  The [[Shape_theory_(mathematics)#Warsaw_Circle|Warsaw circle]] is a path-connected continuum that is not locally path-connected. A ''subcontinuum'' <math>C'</math> of a continuum <math>C</math> is a [[closed set|closed]], connected subset of <math>C</math>. A space is ''nondegenerate'' if it is not equal to a single point. A continuum <math>C</math> is ''decomposable'' if there exist two subcontinua <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> of <math>C</math> such that <math>A \neq C</math> and <math>B \neq C</math> but <math>A \cup B = C</math>. It follows that <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> are nondegenerate. A continuum that is not decomposable is an ''indecomposable continuum''. A continuum <math>C</math> in which every subcontinuum is indecomposable is said to be ''hereditarily indecomposable''. A ''[[composant]]'' of an indecomposable continuum <math>C</math> is a maximal set in which any two points lie within some proper subcontinuum of <math>C</math>. A continuum <math>C</math> is ''irreducible between <math>c</math> and <math>c'</math>'' if  <math>c, c' \in C</math> and no proper subcontinuum contains both points. For a nondegenerate indecomposable metric continuum <math>X</math>, there exists an uncountable subset <math>J</math> such that <math>X</math> is irreducible between any two points of <math>J</math>.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Nadler|first1=Sam|title=Continuum Theory: An Introduction|date=2017|publisher=CRC Press|isbn=9781351990530|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1R8uDwAAQBAJ|language=en}}</ref>

==History==
[[File:Lakes of Wada.png|frame|left|Fifth stage of the Lakes of Wada]] In 1910 L. E. J. Brouwer described an indecomposable continuum that disproved a conjecture made by [[Arthur Moritz Schoenflies]] that, if <math>X_1</math> and <math>X_2</math> are open, connected, disjoint sets in <math>\mathbb{R}^2</math> such that <math>\partial X_1 = \partial X_2</math>, then <math>\partial X_1 = \partial X_2</math> must be the union of two closed, connected proper subsets.<ref>{{citation|journal=Mathematische Annalen
|year=1910|volume= 68|issue =3|pages=422–434
|title=Zur Analysis Situs
|first=L. E. J.|last= Brouwer|doi=10.1007/BF01475781|s2cid=120836681|url=https://zenodo.org/record/2374076}}</ref> [[Zygmunt Janiszewski]] described more such indecomposable continua, including a version of the bucket handle. Janiszewski, however, focused on the irreducibility of these continua. In 1917 [[Kunizo Yoneyama]] described the [[Lakes of Wada]] (named after [[Takeo Wada]]) whose common boundary is indecomposable. In the 1920s indecomposable continua began to be studied by the [[Warsaw School (mathematics)|Warsaw School of Mathematics]] in ''[[Fundamenta Mathematicae]]'' for their own sake, rather than as pathological counterexamples. [[Stefan Mazurkiewicz]] was the first to give the definition of indecomposability. In 1922 [[Bronisław Knaster]] described the [[pseudo-arc]], the first example found of a hereditarily indecomposable continuum.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Cook|first1=Howard|last2=Ingram|first2=William T.|last3=Kuperberg|first3=Krystyna|last4=Lelek|first4=Andrew|last5=Minc|first5=Piotr|title=Continua: With the Houston Problem Book|date=1995|publisher=CRC Press|isbn=9780824796501|pages=103|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bVcZGMOA4AEC&pg=PA103|language=en}}</ref>

== Bucket handle example==
Indecomposable continua are often constructed as the limit of a sequence of nested intersections, or (more generally) as the [[inverse limit]] of a sequence of continua. The buckethandle, or Brouwer–Janiszewski–Knaster continuum, is often considered the simplest example of an indecomposable continuum, and can be so constructed (see upper right). Alternatively, take the [[Cantor ternary set]] <math>\mathcal{C}</math> projected onto the interval <math>[0,1]</math> of the <math>x</math>-axis in the plane. Let <math>\mathcal{C}_0</math> be the family of semicircles above the <math>x</math>-axis with center <math>(1/2,0)</math> and with endpoints on <math>\mathcal{C}</math> (which is symmetric about this point). Let <math>\mathcal{C}_1</math> be the family of semicircles below the <math>x</math>-axis with center the midpoint of the interval <math>[2/3,1]</math> and with endpoints in <math>\mathcal{C} \cap [2/3,1]</math>. Let <math>\mathcal{C}_i</math> be the family of semicircles below the <math>x</math>-axis with center the midpoint of the interval <math>[2/3^i,3/3^i]</math> and with endpoints in <math>\mathcal{C} \cap [2/3^i,3/3^i]</math>. Then the union of all such <math>\mathcal{C}_i</math> is the bucket handle.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Ingram|first1=W. T.|last2=Mahavier|first2=William S.|title=Inverse Limits: From Continua to Chaos|date=2011|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=9781461417972|pages=16|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=II3W2CZxDYMC&pg=PA16|language=en}}</ref> 

The bucket handle admits no Borel transversal, that is there is no [[Borel set]] containing exactly one point from each composant.

==Properties==

In a sense, 'most' continua are indecomposable. Let <math>M</math> be an [[K-cell_(mathematics)|<math>n</math>-cell]] with [[Metric (mathematics)|metric]] <math>d</math>, <math>2^M</math> the set of all nonempty closed subsets of <math>M</math>, and <math>C(M)</math> the ''hyperspace'' of all connected members of <math>2^M</math> equipped with the [[Hausdorff metric]] <math>H_d</math> defined by <math>H_d(A,B) = \max\{\sup\{d(a, B) : a \in A\}, \sup\{d(b, A) : b \in B\}\}</math>. Then the set of nondegenerate indecomposable subcontinua of <math>M</math> is [[Dense set|dense]] in <math>C(M)</math>.

==In dynamical systems==

In 1932 [[George Birkhoff]] described his "remarkable closed curve", a homeomorphism of the [[annulus (mathematics)|annulus]] that contained an invariant continuum. [[Marie Charpentier]] showed that this continuum was indecomposable, the first link from indecomposable continua to dynamical systems. The [[invariant set]] of a certain [[Stephen Smale|Smale]] [[horseshoe map]] is the bucket handle. [[Marcy Barge]] and others have extensively studied indecomposable continua in dynamical systems.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Kennedy|first1=Judy|title=How Indecomposable Continua Arise in Dynamical Systems|journal=Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences|date=1 December 1993|volume=704|issue=1|pages=180–201|doi=10.1111/j.1749-6632.1993.tb52522.x|bibcode=1993NYASA.704..180K|s2cid=85143246|language=en|issn=1749-6632}}</ref>
